pr_comments:
You read my mind, I was precisely working on this. I noticed it produces an arguably better error when trying to load internal modules:
  
  ```console
  $ node -p "require('internal/test/binding')"
  Error: Cannot find module 'internal/test/binding'
  $ node -p "require('node:internal/test/binding')"
  Error: Should not compile internal/test/binding for public use
  ```
  
Can you add tests in `test/parallel/test-require-node-prefix.js`  to make sure requiring internal modules still throws please?
cc @nodejs/modules

> Also would like more @nodejs/modules and @nodejs/tsc eyes on this.

It would also be worth to discuss the semverness of this change before landing.
I still think it is a very bad idea to introduce an inconsistency in caching of CJS modules, including existing core modules.

> I still think it is a very bad idea to introduce an inconsistency in caching of CJS modules, including existing core modules.

My point is that it is already inconsistent and I don't see it becoming more/less consistent with this change. I do see it as a *change* but change itself does not mean inconsistency. With the change at least a programmer can avoid accidents like `fs` vs `fs/` going to different systems. That seems like it would reduce overall inconsistency in a way.

That the system may already have variances doesn’t mean introducing more is costless.

Programmers aren’t going to _want_ to type the extra protocol every time, and imo won’t care enough about the interaction with caching to have that influence their choice - “fs” is shorter than “node:fs” so that’s what will be most popular. However, tooling (linters, build tools/bundlers, resolvers, instrumentation) will now likely have to encode yet another quirk into their already-complex logic instead of just adding core module aliases, to handle the different caching behavior.

> However, tooling (linters, build tools/bundlers, resolvers, instrumentation) will now likely have to encode yet another quirk into their already-complex logic instead of just adding core module aliases, to handle the different caching behavior.

This is true of plenty of new features? I think stating it has a cost is natural. I think the cost itself has some utility that gives programmers writing libraries/applications more expression and I value that over the cost. I am not making a judgement on stating a UX is inferior since having a differing behavior has benefits and trade-offs that come with using it.
Is the different caching behavior marketed here as a new feature? Who does it benefit?

I am starting to think that we need write ups on how tooling can deal w/ these specifiers, and in particular if they should do things like have `node:http` defer to  `node:http` in the cache before `http` before loading the native module etc.

Without the cache bypass behavior, the way for everyone to handle it is just “remove the node: and do the same thing”. With the bypass, it’s potentially much more complicated. For tooling that’s designed to replace core modules via the cache, they’d just break.

I’d still love to understand why the bypass behavior is desired here. Who is it benefiting?

@ljharb regardless of it being seen as a pro or con, any integration of these specifiers will have to integrate in a special way with tooling. They have to strip `node:` properly at the minimum, but if we integrate with the cache the behavior becomes more complex.

* If we migrate `node:fs` to the `fs` cache key that doesn't really match current behavior and I'd rather more expect a `node:fs` cache key lookup.
* Looking for `node:fs` as a key would break existing tools that populate the `require.cache` for builtins preemptively (do we have a concrete example of something doing this? how do they handle the `/` containing builtins these days or in older node versions?)
* If we treat the specifiers as not going through the cache programmers can get some certainty about the source of the module when using the native module system. In some runtime cases, like Jest mentioned above, they replace the entire module system with their own; same for various ahead of time tooling.

So, no matter what introducing the feature adds friction. The question is can we benefit programmers and how much would break if they do use the new feature. We lack a write up on what tooling should do so right now I think the lack of clarity makes it hard to weigh this.

> I’d still love to understand why the bypass behavior is desired here. Who is it benefiting?

People that want to not allow runtime alteration of what `fs` means, in general recreating a new module system entirely or using policies etc. would let it be altered, but code injection couldn't alter what it means.
Isn’t “people want to disallow something” something policies should be handling?

> Isn’t “people want to disallow something” something policies should be handling?

Policies are not an all encompassing feature that seeks to control every bit of code. They are just a configuration mechanism and I don't think altering specific behaviors internal to require is a light ask. So, in this case at least I don't think it would be the easiest choice to deploy, nor the right place to add a hook.
If you don’t want to alter what fs means, can you not require it, freeze it, and defineProperty its cache entry, all in first-run code?

> all in first-run code?

Not everyone is in first-run code.

Also, wouldn't freezing the property in `require.cache` have conflicts with code expecting it to be replaced? So you couldn't have both code wanting the original and wanting the patched form in the same codebase?

It’s JavaScript. If you’re not first-run code, you shouldn’t expect to be able to lock anything down.

The desire to lock things down is what causes conflicts with things attempting to replace it - there’s no patching case i know of where it’s acceptable to *permit* other code to bypass the patching. In other words, just like polyfills, it has to be global and the original must be impossible to obtain. This PR breaks polyfilling.

> The desire to lock things down is what causes conflicts with things attempting to replace it - there’s no patching case i know of where it’s acceptable to permit other code to bypass the patching. In other words, just like polyfills, it has to be global and the original must be impossible to obtain. This PR breaks polyfilling.

To be clear, polyfilling using `require.cache` doesn't actually replace the module completely, use a complete module system replacement (as jest, esm, etc. do) or use policies. I don't think arguing for compatibility with something on the basis of an incomplete replacement is a good idea. Figuring out how to do a complete replacement seems a better path forward to me.

I see both Jordan's and Bradley's point and I think it makes sense to ask tools to weigh in.

Let's try @SimenB maybe? What do you think? The tl;dr; is:

 - Node is introducing `node:fs` prefixed to make it explicit a module is coming from Node.js core and not userland in CommonJS modules.
 - Node is contemplating bypassing the require cache in those cases (so `require('node:fs')` is always native FS.

Is this fine given Jest already replaces require? Does it create any problems for you?

(Other readers - please consider pinging maintainers you know :))

Also to be explicit: I am still blocking (hopefully for not too long).

I feel like the discussion about caching hasn't exhausted itself and it's a big point - please don't land this until discussion has concluded. If discussion dies and no conclusive decision is made - I will unblock regardless.
To be clear I am not blocking if it is changed to match, but would want a thorough write-up for tooling to be able to properly handle these if we do change it.
(I actually think the skipping-the-cache behaviour is interesting and while I see Jordan's point if tooling is in favour of keeping it and tools like jest/esm don't mind - I think it's a win)

Thanks for the ping! 👍 

>Is this fine given Jest already replaces require? Does it create any problems for you?

~Jest uses `resolve`'s `isCoreModule`~ (see edit), so resolution doesn't matter for us as long as that returns `true`*. Caching - we have given up evaluating Node core modules ourselves (although please pick up #31852 😀 ) and just pass it through to the "real" one. So we already always return the "core" module (at least in theory). We allow people to do `jest.mock('fs')`, but that happens before any resolution, so shouldn't matter in this case.

*) https://github.com/facebook/jest/blob/fedafc3c974d0aa06078f6122a3341a0f37e98f7/packages/jest-runtime/src/index.ts#L600-L602 & https://github.com/facebook/jest/blob/fedafc3c974d0aa06078f6122a3341a0f37e98f7/packages/jest-runtime/src/index.ts#L1230-L1240

(I just read the tl;dr (thanks for that!), so probably a bunch of context I might be missing)

EDIT: Oops, we don't use `resolve`'s `isCore`, we use `module.builtinModules`: https://github.com/facebook/jest/blob/fedafc3c974d0aa06078f6122a3341a0f37e98f7/packages/jest-resolve/src/isBuiltinModule.ts
@SimenB would you see any issues or concerns with `jest.mock('fs')` also intercepting these specifier with the `node:` prefix?

@bmeck not beyond 2 specifiers being used for the same module. I.e. `jest.mock('fs')` _not_ mocking `node:fs` and vice versa. If you added `aliasedModules` or something along with `builtinModules` on the `module`... module we can probably resolve that cleanly? Or is that ``builtinModules.map(m => `node:${m}`)``? Which means all older versions of jest would return the wrong module in the mocking case

```mjs
builtinModules.map(m => node:`${m}`)
```

Seems like it would suffice in either direction we move forward here.
Ping @arcanis for Yarn PnP: if `require('node:fs')` bypasses the require cache, is it going to cause issues?

Interesting - it depends; the relevant part of the code is [here](https://github.com/yarnpkg/berry/blob/master/packages/yarnpkg-pnp/sources/loader/applyPatch.ts#L72-L81). If we detect that the module is a builtin (by checking the public `builtinModules`), then it goes in the regular Node loader, which will bypass the patch and follow Node's logic. Otherwise, we run into our own cache layer (required in order to avoid potential conflicts when a same runtime uses two dependency tree sharing the same package location).

So if `builtinModules` is updated to also contain the `node:<name>` identifiers it should Just Work™, otherwise we'll have to update our code to take this into account.

That being said, note that to support @ljharb's point:

> The desire to lock things down is what causes conflicts with things attempting to replace it - there’s no patching case i know of where it’s acceptable to _permit_ other code to bypass the patching. In other words, just like polyfills, it has to be global and the original must be impossible to obtain. This PR breaks polyfilling.

We apply a filesystem layer adding support for zip archives by patching the result of `require('fs')` so that packages doing filesystem calls into themselves can work transparently (in lack of better ways, ref https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/36812). If `node:fs` becomes the "preferred way" / "good practice" to access the Node primitives, I hope this use case will still be supported / covered by tests.

> Or is it the same result as normal but you replace properties on the `fs` module? The intent here is not to prevent patching the `fs` module properties, just the reference to it.

Same result, the functions are just [replaced](https://github.com/yarnpkg/berry/blob/master/packages/yarnpkg-fslib/sources/patchFs.ts#L87-L99). We noticed that completely replacing the object itself wasn't a good idea anyway since the core Node methods (like those in `Module._extensions`) wouldn't use them (unfortunately you've started to replace the `fs.something` calls by destructuring, and that makes that more fragile 😅 I should open an issue about this).

Adding the `semver-minor` label. Note that this PR would be a breaking change for a user using a package whose name starts with `node:` – that kind of package wouldn't be hosted on npm, wouldn't work well with ESM, and would have limited support on Windows anyway.

> Adding the `semver-minor` label. Note that this PR would be a breaking change for a user using a package whose name starts with `node:` – that kind of package wouldn't be hosted on npm, wouldn't work well with ESM, and would have limited support on Windows anyway.

If it's breaking it should be `semver-major`.

FWIW for anyone curious about Windows the ":" denotes an alternate data stream on NTFS. See https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/34895#issuecomment-707388054 for a demonstration on how it can be (ab)used.

It's arguably a breaking change for users of Jest doing `jest.mock('fs')`, expecting (rightly) that to mock all fs usage, but some dependency starts using `node:fs`. Not sure if that should be considered "breaking" for node itself?

If it's decided to do this (adding `node:*`) I can add support to Jest so at least from the next release (v27, hopefully stable this month) it'll work correctly. But it'll still be breaking IMO for older versions.

I assume it's also a breaking change for user of others mocking systems, like `proxyquire` etc?

> I assume it's also a breaking change for user of others mocking systems, like proxyquire etc?

It would likely not match user expectations / require support for the feature to be added if that is what is being asked. However, no existing code would break, only usage of the new feature would break things. This seems semver minor since it is like any other API addition we do. It would be good to understand why is broken by adding the API itself.

> If it's breaking it should be `semver-major`.

Fair enough, I think the way forward is to land this PR as `semver-major`, then to open a backport PR to `v15.x-staging` to discuss the possibility of introducing it as `semver-minor` in v15.x and v14.x. In that case, this needs (at least) one more approval from a @nodejs/tsc member.

TBH I don't think this should land as `Semver-Major`. I think we should land as `Semver-Minor`, release it on 15 and see what ends up happening in the ecosystem. If we are "very concerned" that it could cause lots of issues we could always release with 16.x, skip landing it on 15.x, and let it bake for a couple months before determining if we want to backport to 14 (as we do with any other Semver-Minor features).

I just now realized out that this is about adding support for `node:` prefix in _`require`_ and that it already works for ESM imports. First I've heard of this prefix is this PR 😅 

Since that's the case the "breakage" I was concerned about has already happened, so (fwiw) I'm fine with this landing as a minor.

---

As an aside, using `node:` doesn't work in Jest (it throws `Module not found`) since it "fools" our "is this node core" check due to it not existing in `builtinModules`. I guess the proper solution is to map over them and add the `node:` prefix?

`resolve` also fails

```sh-session
$ node -p 'require("resolve").isCore("node:fs")'
false
```

`resolve` only resolves CJS, so it's supposed to fail right now. (Landing this is arguably semver-major for this reason, among others) after this lands, and i know which node version it will release in, i'll update `is-core-module` to include all the `node:`-prefixed modules.

I use `builtinModules` in tests to validate the results, so it would be really helpful if that were updated with all the `node:` variants as well.

@ljharb `is-core-module` [relies on a lookup](https://github.com/inspect-js/is-core-module/blob/main/core.json) to determine if a module is a core module afaict. With this in mind adding `node:` is no more breaking than adding any new core module.
@MylesBorins yes, the builtinModules comment was just to make my tests easier, it doesn’t affect the implementation.

I've gone ahead and changed the label from `Semver-Major` > `Semver-Minor`... I've also added the labels `lts-watch-v14.x` and `baking-for-lts` so we don't forget about discussing this in a future 14.x minor. Finally I added the `do-not-land-v15.x` label to ensure this only goes out on 16.x

I think that this satisfied the concerns folks have about rolling this out into the ecosystem too quickly while also ensuring that it accurately reflects the semveriness of the change.
Landed in b079960b1844...95391fe689ec

A lint error was introduced in modules.md with these commits. 

Please fast-track the PR to fix this: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/37811

(Not sure if they were in the regular PR or in a last-minute rebase or caused by some weird ships-crossing-in-the-night interaction with another PR that landed. Not terribly concerned. These things happen. But would like it fixed for an onboarding in a few hours!)
@ExE-Boss do you mind creating a backport PR for this one? It didn't land cleanly on `v14.x-staging`. Thanks!

@danielleadams I think we should maybe wait a little bit before backporting this to v14.x. It was originally labelled at Semver-Major but we opted to land as Semver-Minor and get some feedback first. I think this makes more sense for the 14.18.0 release rather than 14.17.0

issue_context.title: Add support for `node:`‑prefixed imports of built‑in modules to `require(…)`
issue_context.body: See the [**2020‑10‑29 TSC Meeting notes**](https://github.com/nodejs/TSC/blob/master/meetings/2020-10-29.md#nodejsnode), where it was decided that **CommonJS** should also support `node:`‑prefixed imports, so that any future built‑in modules (e.g.: [`diagnostics_channel`](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/34895)) don’t risk possible ecosystem breakage.

review_comments:
This bifurcation will have implications for mocking, but I can appreciate the benefit too.

I'd still prefer a more convergent path here eg, to return `node:fs` for both `node:fs` and `fs` inputs, and then to still populate a `cache['fs']` entry in the `node:fs` case as the same object for backwards compatibility. Such a change would hopefully be mostly compatible but would probably need to be a separate major nontheless. Worth thinking about at least.

Existing mocking tools (such as **Jest**) provide their own `require(…)` implementation, since they need to be able to bypass the mocked module using [jest.requireActual(…)](https://jestjs.io/docs/en/bypassing-module-mocks).

What is the motivation for short-circuiting the cache here, something that has never been done previously for native modules?

I don't see why this scheme should be any different to any other in this regard.
On this topic, should we throw or defer to cache on unknown builtins?
this differs from other builtins, I love it, but want to be sure it is intentional.

this actually seems like an issue - it means someone who replaces a builtin intentionally can’t replace one of these (altho presumably mutating a builtin would be visible in both). That could cause an issue where someone wants to use a package to instrument or lock down `fs` (and thus, policies are not an ergonomic option, unless I’m misunderstanding how policies work), but accidentally leaves a gaping security hole when an attacker requires `node:fs`.

policies should intercept before any of the resolution helpers even get called https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/36cc0ee993a07174f47ea598b6c2c75a66cb052c/lib/internal/modules/cjs/helpers.js#L52 , if any module redirection is in place (including complete shutdown) then it would never call out to `module.require` and get here without some kind of opt-in to the behavior (like `dependencies:true`).
At the very least this needs documentation and probably a strong indication people using policies + instrumenting fs now need to update the policy.

My point was that policies aren’t currently required to ensure this for CJS - a package (not the app itself) can do it. Forcing policies to be the mechanism means packages are no longer capable of abstracting this for users.
@ljharb ah, yes that is true. I just wanted to be clear that policies can prevent this intentionally and should not be considered to have support for such a workflow.

Totally understood. Given that policies are the superior mechanism for app developers to lock things down, what's the benefit of adding special, inconsistent, cache-bypassing behavior for `require` with a `node:` prefix?

@ljharb i have no strong opinion on if we should diverge, but cache first behavior of CJS isn't shared by ESM and isn't robust against things like core destructuring the original impls. My like is just that it isn't a confusing situation like with `fs/`.
indeed, but that doesn’t mean it’s a good idea to make CJS inconsistent with itself.

I don't think CJS is able to be claimed as consistent with itself since in general the natives don't normally populate the cache. I think it was just ad-hoc written together and the cache behavior is evolutionary not intentional or well understood (even by me).
